title: Mahesha Pandita
html:
Mahabahu, Krishna's Friend

Mahesha Pandita is one of the twelve cowherd boys, the gopalas, who came into Gaura's pastimes together with Nityananda. The biographies call him Sri Mahesha Pandita; Krishnadasa Kaviraja calls him Mahesha Pandita and simply Mahesha; Vrindavana Dasa, Mahesha Pandita; Narahari Chakravarti, Pandita Mahesha and Mahesha. Who he is in Krishna's eternal pastimes, Kavi Karnapura tells us:

“Subahu, a cowherd of Vraja, is Uddharana Datta; Mahabahu, a friend in Vraja, is Sriman Mahesha Pandita.” (GGD 129)

Mahabahu is a friend (sakha) of Krishna, a cowherd boy of Vraja. This is not the former birth of an ordinary soul who in time became a devotee, nor is it imitation of a cowherd boy: an eternal associate, bound to Krishna in friendship (sakhya-rasa), appeared in Gaura-lila together with his Lord Nityananda — the Balarama of Vraja — to serve Him here as well.

In the “Anubhashya” Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati counts him seventh among the twelve gopalas, and the biographies count him the same way: in the order of the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” he is preceded by Abhirama, Sundarananda, Dhananjaya, Gauridasa, Kamalakara and Uddharana.1 All twelve are given seats of honour in the Vishva-vaishnava-raja-sabha, the assembly of the Vaishnavas of the whole world. The order of names in the lists of gopalas is not always the same, however, and in one of them Mahesha stands tenth.2

On the tree of Sri Chaitanya drawn by Krishnadasa Kaviraja, Mahesha Pandita is named twice. Among the branches of Mahaprabhu Himself:

“Subuddhi Mishra, Hridayananda, Kamala-nayana, Mahesha Pandita, Shrikara, Sri Madhusudana.” (CC, Adi 10.111)

And among the branches of Nityananda:

“Mahesha Pandita is a generous cowherd boy of Vraja; to the beat of the kettledrum he would dance, drunk with love.” (CC, Adi 11.32)

So the biographies count him as a branch both of Sri Chaitanya and of Sri Nityananda.3

Birthplace and Brothers

Little is known of Mahesha's family and birthplace. One of the biographies takes present-day Chakdaha in Nadia to be his birthplace, but at once adds that there is no reliable evidence for this.

Some hold him to have been Jagadisha Pandita's youngest brother; Jagadisha's shripata is at Yashada, not far from those parts. On this view the brothers were three: Jagadisha the eldest, Hiranya the middle one, and Mahesha the youngest. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta, writing of Jagadisha, gives the tradition of his shripata at Yashada: when Jagadisha's parents had departed from this world, he left his homeland together with his wife Dukhini and his brother Mahesha and settled in Mayapur, next to the house of Sri Jagannatha Mishra. But whether that Mahesha is Mahesha Pandita, Mahabahu of Vraja, the authoritative books, he remarks, do not say, “and therefore it is doubtful.”4 Yet one of the biographies tells it as settled fact that it was Mahesha Pandita, his youngest brother, who went to the Ganges with Jagadisha and his wife.5

Nityananda's Companion

Mahesha Pandita was a companion (parshada) of Sri Nityananda and, in the words of one of the biographies, a friend particularly close to Him. Like all who surrounded Nityananda, he was generous beyond measure and laboured for the deliverance of fallen souls. This does not mean that the servant became equal to his Lord: the mercy he gave away was the mercy of Nityananda Himself, flowing through His companion.

Vrindavana Dasa Thakura, listing Nityananda's servants, says of him:

“Mahesha Pandita was a most exalted great soul.” (CB, Antya 5.744)

In Bengali — ati parama mahanta, “the very greatest of great devotees.”6 And the vandana ascribed to Vrindavana Dasa himself adds that he is especially dear to Nityananda.

How he is remembered can be seen from the verse of the “Charitamrita” quoted above: he danced to the beat of the kettledrum (dhaka), drunk with love. This is the madness of divine love, prema-unmada, not worldly frenzy: so the eternal friendship of a cowherd boy of Vraja with Krishna shows itself in Gaura-lila. Srila Jiva Gosvami too, in his vandana, praises “Mahesha Pandita, overwhelmed by madness for Krishna,” and the Bengali vandanas praise him in the same way: Devakinandana Dasa as “a great madman [of love],” and the vandana of the “second” Vrindavana Dasa as “maddened by Krishna”; both place him beside Jagadisha Pandita. His name also stands in Devakinandana's list of Vaishnavas.

In Narahari Chakravarti's “Namamrita-samudra,” a book of prayers to the Lord's associates, Mahesha is named beside Kamalakara Pippalai:

“Sri Kamalakara Piplai, O Mahesha, hear me! Deliver this unworthy one, and your fame will be proclaimed without end.” (“Namamrita-samudra” 37)

In the “Chaitanya-mangala” Lochana Dasa names Mahesha Pandita among the companions gathered around Gauranga in Navadvipa when the Lord was giving away prema: “Sri Rama Pandita and Mahesha Pandita, Haridasa, Nandana Acharya — the righteous…” (Madhya 24.59).7

Panihati and Saptagrama

When Nityananda held the festival of flat rice with yogurt (chida-dadhi) at Panihati for Raghunatha Dasa, Mahesha was among His companions. Krishnadasa Kaviraja lists those seated around Nityananda on the platform:

“Ramadasa, Sundarananda, Gadadhara Dasa, Murari, Kamalakara, Sadashiva, Purandara, Dhananjaya, Jagadisha, Parameshvara Dasa, Mahesha, Gauridasa, Krishnadasa Hoda.” (CC, Antya 6.61–62)

After the festival Mahesha Pandita followed Nityananda to Saptagrama — so Srila Bhaktisiddhanta says in the “Anubhashya.”8

After the Lord's Disappearance

Mahesha Pandita remained in this world even after Mahaprabhu and Nityananda had withdrawn Their pastimes. We meet him in Khardaha, in Nityananda's house, where Vasudha and Jahnava lived with Virabhadra. When Srinivasa came there and stayed four or five days, the devotees of Khardaha showered their mercy on him:

“Suryadasa, Gauridasa, Pandita Mahesha — many devotees there showed him boundless mercy.” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 4.91)

After that Jahnava and Virabhadra told Srinivasa to go to Vrindavana.

Later Narottama came to Khardaha. He was on his way to Nilachala; in Saptagrama he had learned that Uddharana Datta had already departed from this world, and he went on, visiting the homes of devotees along the road. In the “Narottama-vilasa” Narahari Chakravarti tells us that the first to notice him were Mahesha Pandita and others:

“At that moment Mahesha Pandita and others, from afar, seeing Narottama, said softly: ‘In separation from Prabhu we have become as if dead, yet at the sight of him happiness arises in the heart. Without Prabhu's power this would not be possible.’” (“Narottama-vilasa” 3.176–178)

Learning who stood before them, they told Narottama that they had long heard of him: how he had left home for Vrindavana, how on the way back the books had been stolen and recovered, how he had come to Navadvipa — “that is why we are still alive — to see you with our own eyes” (3.182). Narottama wept and rolled at their feet, and they embraced him, bathed him in tears and at last, growing calm, brought him into Prabhu's house, where Vasudha and Jahnava at once called him to them (3.183–187).

For two to four days Narottama was not allowed to leave Khardaha. Virabhadra spoke with him, Parameshvari Dasa showed him the road, and when Jahnava gave him leave to go to Nilachala,

“Mahesha Pandita and others dear to Prabhu embraced Narottama again and again. All bade him go to Nilachala, and Narottama bowed at the feet of all.” (“Narottama-vilasa” 3.200–201)

Having gone with him a little way, the weeping devotees returned home. Narahari speaks of this in the “Bhakti-ratnakara” as well:

“Mahesha Pandita and the others, having seen Narottama off in great affection, could not regain their calm.” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 8.220)9

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta likewise notes, citing the eighth wave of the “Bhakti-ratnakara,” that Mahesha Pandita was in Khardaha when Narottama came there.

More than once Narottama saw Mahesha when the Lord revealed His pastimes to him in dreams. Before he had even left home he dreamt of the sankirtana of Gaura, Nityananda and Advaita on the bank of the Ganges in Navadvipa, and among the companions were “Mahesha, Shankara, Yadu, Acharya-nandana” (“Narottama-vilasa” 2.123); and in Puri, in a dream before the chariot, among the Lord's companions were “Gauridasa, Mahesha Pandita, Damodara” (4.129).

And at the great festival in Kheturi, when Narottama began the kirtan, Mahaprabhu by His own will appeared there with all His companions, and everyone saw Him. Among the dancing companions the “Narottama-vilasa” names Mahesha too: “Jagadisha, Suryadasa, Acharya-nandana, Shrinatha, Mahesha, Yadu, Sri Madhusudana…” (7.119); so too the “Bhakti-ratnakara” (10.595). This was no vision or product of imagination, but a real pastime of the Lord, who fulfilled what He had promised Narottama in a dream. Whether Mahesha was in Kheturi in person or came with the Lord among the companions who had already departed, the texts do not say outright: “the manifest and the unmanifest came together in one place” (“Narottama-vilasa” 7.123).10

Departure

Mahesha Pandita disappeared — departed from this world — on the thirteenth lunar day of the dark fortnight of the month of Pausha (krishna-trayodashi); on this the biographies agree. In the Vaishnava calendar of the Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math it is the Krishna-trayodashi of the month of Narayana; it will next fall on 5 January 2027, and on the same day the departure of Srila Uddharana Datta Thakura is honoured — the very Subahu whom Karnapura names in the same verse with him. The sources name neither the year nor the place of his departure, nor the day of his appearance; nor do they speak of the place of his samadhi, apart from the memorial altar at the shripata described below.

The Shripata

Mahesha Pandita's first shripata was at Masipur (Srila Bhaktisiddhanta adds, not quite certainly: “or Yashipur”), on the Ganges' eastern bank, opposite Jirat. The Ganges swallowed Masipur, and the Deity installed by Mahesha Pandita was moved for a time to Beledanga near Sukhsagar. When the river ate away Beledanga too, the zamindar of Palpara, Navakumara Chattopadhyaya, persuaded the servitor of the day, the babaji Ramakrishnadasa, to bring the Deity to Palpara, and built a temple there. His son Rajani Babu in 1883 deeded the temple lands to Harekrishnadasa Babaji; hence the name “Palpara-pat.”

Palpara lies in Nadia district, in the forest, a mile south of Chakdaha station; the Ganges, as Srila Bhaktisiddhanta writes, is far from here.11 This is the pargana of Panchanagar: it has fourteen villages (mauzas) — Beledanga, Berigram, Sukhsagar, Chandure, Manasapota, Palpara and others — and some call this country “Nagardesh.”

The shripata remained in Palpara until the first months of the Bengali year 1334 (1927) and was then moved to Kathalpuli (Kathaldhuli) near Chakdaha; the move was reported in the journal “Gaudiya” (year 6, no. 13, “Letters received”).12 On 28 June 1931 Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati formally took over the management of Mahesha Pandita's shripata in Chakdaha and spoke at the opening before a large gathering. In the list of maths and preaching centres founded by Srila Bhaktisiddhanta the shripata appears as number 22: “Shripata of Sri Mahesha Pandita, Kathalpuli, P.O. Chakdaha, Nadia.”

The temple of the shripata is a modest building, like an ordinary dwelling house, and already in the days of the “Anubhashya” it was dilapidated. In it reside Sri Gopinatha, Sri Radha-Govinda, Sri Madana-mohana, Sri Gaura-Nityananda and a shalagrama-shila — the Lord Himself, manifest as the archa-vigraha to accept the service of His devotees. Before the temple stands the altar of the phul-samaj, the “flower tomb” of Mahesha Pandita — a memorial place where his presence is honoured.13

In Srila Bhaktisiddhanta's time the service was kept up only by alms: a local resident, Sri Kalikrishna Chakravarti, gave twenty-five rupees a year towards it, and the servitor was Sri Sanatana Dasa Babaji. Mahesha Pandita left no descendants.

Significance

The original sources say little of Mahesha Pandita, yet it is enough to let us see who he was. In Vraja he is Mahabahu, Krishna's friend; in Gaura's pastimes, one of the twelve gopalas, a servant of Nityananda and, in Vrindavana Dasa's words, “the very greatest of great devotees.” His dancing to the kettledrum is the madness of the pure prema of a cowherd boy of Vraja; his generosity to the fallen is Nityananda's mercy flowing through His companion. And when the Lord withdrew His pastimes, Mahesha and his fellows, by their own words, lived only in the hope of seeing the Lord's new devotees — and on seeing Narottama they found their joy again.

Let us pray, then, for the mercy of Mahesha Pandita — Mahabahu of Vraja, Krishna's friend and Nityananda's companion.
